TEN-1.title: Tenant comes from the credential only
TEN-1.mechanism: the prohibition half IS built and proven on all four surfaces: `scanEndpointSpine` rejects tenant-shaped route, query and body-contract names by tokenized run, and a runtime `onRequest` strip in `createApp` removes tenant-shaped request headers before any handler, which is the only reachable mechanism for a surface that cannot be closed. The strip's registry carries the concatenated spellings (`tenantid`, `orgid`, `organisationid`) explicitly, because Node lowercases header names before any hook runs, so `X-TenantId` arrives as `x-tenantid` and the tokenizer's camel-case half is unavailable on this surface by construction
TEN-1.note: Lifted off `owed` 2026-07-27 at 53b1eec, and the roll-up rule is what lifted it: the mint half of SEC-4 and TEN-6 is still owed, but the VERIFY half landed 2026-07-27 at 53b1eec and moved the second obligation off `owed`. TEN-1's statement is a prohibition plus a resolution rule; the prohibition is realized and red-green proven, and the resolution rule had no mechanism for as long as no credential existed to resolve from, which is S-8. It has one now. Round 4 audit: the prohibition half was itself overstated, because `X-TenantId` and `X-OrgId` walked past the strip over real HTTP until the concatenated entries landed, which is evidence for the conservative status rather than against it. Findings: A-2, E-9, E-10, S-8.

obligations.name: tenant identity never travels as a request parameter
obligations.text: `scanEndpointSpine` rejects tenant-shaped route, query and body-contract names by tokenized run, and a runtime `onRequest` strip in `createApp` removes tenant-shaped headers before any handler, carrying the concatenated spellings explicitly because Node lowercases header names before any hook runs.

obligations.name: the tenant is resolved solely from the validated credential
obligations.text: Built 2026-07-27 at 53b1eec, and it is the S-8 gap closing. The trigger, the credential mint, has half fired: this edition now VERIFIES a credential even though it still does not mint one, and verification is the half this obligation needed. `decideCredential` reads the Authorization header, verifies the signature, and puts the token's `tenant_id` on a frozen credential; it reads no route parameter, no query value, no body and no other header, and `app.ts` has already deleted every tenant-shaped header before it runs. So a tenant reaching a handler has come through a verified signature and through nothing else. Planted at 53b1eec: a token carrying no `tenant_id`, or an array in its place, is refused rather than defaulted. `patterned` and not `proven` for a reason this row should say plainly: NOTHING DOWNSTREAM READS `request.credential` YET, so the resolution rule is proven at the point of resolution and unexercised at every point of use. The first store query that scopes by tenant is the first seam that has to take it from here rather than from an argument, and each such seam owes its own test.

TEN-5.title: Sanctioned-bypass ledger

All four planted here and all four red-correct: an absent ledger, a row with an empty test cell, a row naming `NightlyNodeSweepIsSoleReader` which exists nowhere, and a second `billing-bypass-ledger.md`. The row stays `owed` on one obligation, and in this edition it is trigger-gated twice over: there is no sanctioned bypass AND there is no persistence layer for one to live in. Findings: E-34, E-35, E-77.

obligations.name: a ledger row that names no sole-reader test fails the build

obligations.name: the named sole-reader test exists, and is the remedy

TEN-6.title: Tenant is minted from membership, never asserted
TEN-6.mechanism: `tokenVerification.ts` refuses a token that does not carry exactly one non-empty `tenant_id`; `bearerCredential.ts` puts it on the credential and reads no other surface; `app.ts` strips every tenant-shaped header before the seam runs
TEN-6.note: Half built 2026-07-27 at 53b1eec. The verifier half of this claim is real: a credential now carries exactly one tenant and it comes from a signed token. The MINT half is what the claim is named for and it needs membership data, which this edition has no store for, so it stays owed and named rather than borrowing credit from the half that landed. Findings: E-84.

obligations.name: the credential carries exactly one active tenant
obligations.text: Planted 2026-07-27 at 53b1eec: a token with no `tenant_id`, or with an array in its place, is refused by reason rather than defaulted, and a verified token's `tenantId` is asserted to be the value the token carried. `Credential` has a single `tenantId` field, so 'exactly one' is the type rather than a convention.

obligations.name: a tenant never travels as a header, a parameter, or mutable session state
obligations.text: Three mechanisms, none of them new here and all of them now load-bearing because there is finally a credential for them to be the alternative to: `app.ts` deletes every tenant-shaped header in the first onRequest hook, before the credential seam; `scanEndpointSpine` refuses a tenant-shaped name on the route, query and body surfaces of the composed table; and `decideCredential` reads the Authorization header and nothing else, so there is no code path by which a tenant reaches a handler except through a verified signature. The credential is frozen, so it is not mutable session state either.

obligations.name: entering or switching a tenant mints a new credential through the real sign-in surface
obligations.text: Unbuilt, and this is the clause the claim is named for. There is no sign-in surface, no tenant selector, and no membership data to validate a selection against, so nothing here mints anything: tokens are minted out of process by the shared harness minter, which is legitimate for a kernel with no identity module and is exactly the premise `mintToken.mjs` records as invalidated by the first identity slice. trigger: a membership store, which arrives with the persistence layer (G); the mint surface is then TEN-1's one sanctioned carve-out and `CARVE_OUTS` in endpointSpine.ts is the empty list waiting for it.

obligations.name: revoking a membership bumps the session version, so credentials for that tenant die immediately
obligations.text: Composes with SEC-4, and SEC-4's half of it is built: `sessionVersions.bump` exists and a bumped principal's token is refused end to end. What is missing is the thing that would CALL it, because there is no membership to revoke. trigger: the same membership store; this obligation is a one-line call at the point where a membership is removed, and it is recorded now so that point is not written without it.

SEC-1.title: Every endpoint gated
SEC-1.mechanism: `POLICIES` registry (a policy naming no permission, or named `anonymous`, is refused at construction, so the bare authenticated-only gate is unrepresentable rather than rejected, and both refusals are exercised by test rather than asserted over the shipped registry's contents); every route declares `config.policy`, checked by `scanEndpointSpine` over the composed table; `ANONYMOUS_ROUTES` carries a justification per entry, is keyed by method and url, covers a synthesized HEAD only under reference identity on `config`, and a stale entry fails; deny-by-default `onRequest` hook installed in the expression that creates the instance, denying an ungated route to anonymous AND authenticated callers alike; `composeApp` runs the scan after `ready()` and refuses to compose a violating surface, which is itself red-green proven through the `surfaces` parameter
SEC-1.note: Re-measured 2026-07-27 (node Phase A) and the flat `proven` is now five obligations, because a flat status is how several separate things come to be carried by one word (the lesson E-72 recorded in the sibling). Every obligation below is evidenced by a permanent test that runs on every suite execution, not by a hand-run pass. The credential mint is still owed (SEC-4, TEN-6), so every gated route in this exemplar answers 401 and the permission evaluation is proven through an injected `authenticate` seam rather than a real mint; that is a limit on what has been exercised end to end, not on the gate. Findings: A-3, A-4, E-7, E-8, E-10, E-79.

obligations.name: every route names a policy, or is an allowlisted anonymous route
obligations.text: `scanEndpointSpine` reads `config.policy` off every entry in the composed table. Four refusals run as permanent tests: no policy at all, an anonymous route absent from the allowlist, a look-alike policy object (policies compare by identity, not shape), and an independently registered HEAD trying to ride in on its GET's allowlist entry. The last has its own non-vacuity partner asserting the SYNTHESIZED head is accepted, so the guard is not simply refusing all HEADs.

obligations.name: the enumeration reaches every route the server serves
obligations.text: Two independent mechanisms, and the second is why this is `proven` and not merely believed. The table records REFERENCES at `onRoute` and materializes at `onReady`, after every hook has had its turn, and `onReady` reconciles it against Fastify's own `printRoutes()` and refuses to boot on a disagreement in either direction. Measured 2026-07-27: narrowing the scan's own loop to match nothing fails 23 tests across SEC-1, SEC-2, SEC-3 and the wiring proof, each naming its claim. The sibling's equivalent narrowing left five assertions across two claims green (E-72), and the difference is structural rather than diligence (E-79).

obligations.name: the anonymous allowlist is reviewed rather than accumulated
obligations.text: Each entry carries a justification, is keyed by method AND url, and a stale entry that matches no route fails, so the list cannot rot. A synthesized HEAD is covered under its GET by REFERENCE identity on `config`, which is a proof of synthesis no comparison of values can give, and is what stops a separately written HEAD from inheriting the carve-out.

obligations.name: the fallback denies by default, to authenticated callers too
obligations.text: The deny-by-default `onRequest` hook is installed in the expression that creates the instance. Proven against both an anonymous caller and an AUTHENTICATED one with no permission, which is the distinction that makes it deny-by-default rather than require-authentication (the sibling shipped the weaker one, E-7). Seven hook bypass attempts and a credential-leak probe were run and none evaded.

obligations.name: the scan is wired into composition, not merely written
obligations.text: `composeApp` runs `assertEndpointSpine` after `ready()`, so a violating surface refuses to BOOT rather than merely failing CI. The wiring is itself red-green proven through the `surfaces` parameter, which exists precisely because the composed app is by construction the one with no violations in it, so a violating surface has to be passable in. An earlier round claimed this refusal on the evidence of a manual injection, and an audit then deleted the call and its import and watched the suite stay green with a clean typecheck and lint.

SEC-2.title: Anti mass-assignment
SEC-2.mechanism: `scanEndpointSpine` walks every route's `schema.body` recursively through `properties`, `items` and `allOf`/`anyOf`/`oneOf`, matching `SERVER_CONTROLLED_FIELDS` by tokenized run (`id` whole-name only, so a foreign key does not trip it); `createApp` refuses at registration any schema keyword the walk does not descend (`$ref`, `patternProperties`, tuple-form `items`, `not`, `if`/`then`/`else`, `dependentSchemas`, `prefixItems`, `contains`, `propertyNames`, `unevaluatedProperties`, `definitions`) and requires EVERY object schema inside a scanned surface to set `additionalProperties: false`, so the closed declaration is a runtime filter at every level and not only at the top
SEC-2.note: Re-measured 2026-07-27 (node Phase A); the flat `proven` is now four obligations. The contract is a value on the route, so there is no assembly heuristic, no name-suffix filter and no route-without-contract (B-2). The registration-time refusal of unwalkable schema keywords is this edition's strongest single mechanism and the sibling has no equivalent of it. Findings: B-2, B-4, E-6, E-9, E-10, E-79.

obligations.name: the predicate rejects a registry member at any depth of a declared body
obligations.text: The walk descends `properties`, `items` and `allOf`/`anyOf`/`oneOf`. Refusals run as permanent tests at the top level and nested, with a non-vacuity partner accepting a body carrying only caller-owned fields. Depth was the round 4 audit's finding: the closure was depth-0 only, so an open nested object delivered `author.tenantId` and `author.createdBy` to the handler with the scan silent.

obligations.name: the enumeration reaches every body-bearing route
obligations.text: Same composed table and same boot-time reconciliation as SEC-1's enumeration obligation, and the same measurement covers it: narrowing the scan's loop fails this claim's tests by name (E-79). Only GET and HEAD are bodyless; the obligation set is inverted rather than enumerated, so a method this code has never heard of owes a body contract rather than escaping.

obligations.name: the declaration cannot hide a surface the walk does not descend
obligations.text: `createApp` refuses at REGISTRATION any schema keyword the walk cannot descend (`$ref`, `patternProperties`, tuple-form `items`, `not`, `if`/`then`/`else`, `dependentSchemas`, `prefixItems`, `contains`, `propertyNames`, `unevaluatedProperties`, `definitions`) and requires every object schema inside a scanned surface to set `additionalProperties: false`. This is the obligation the sibling has no equivalent of: the closed declaration is a runtime filter at every level, not only at the top, so eight evasions found by the round 4 audit are refused at boot rather than reported later.

obligations.name: the comparison resolves compounds, concatenations and decompositions of a listed word
obligations.text: Matched by tokenized run, with `id` whole-name only so a foreign key does not trip it, asserted in both directions: `id` and `Id` match, `parentId` and `noteId` do not. The registry's heuristic residue is the claim's own declared weakening note (a field named `newState` slips past a registry listing `status`), so it is the claim's cost rather than this mechanism's gap.

SEC-3.title: No PII in URLs
SEC-3.mechanism: `scanEndpointSpine` over the composed route table: path parameters reconciled between the URL text and `schema.params` (a disagreement in either direction fails), query parameters from the mandatory closed `schema.querystring`, matched against `PII_PARAMETERS` by tokenized contiguous run so `emailAddress` and `user_email` match `email`, plus explicit entries for the three morphological classes a run over a tokenized entry cannot reach: concatenations (`firstname`, `dateofbirth`), decompositions (`mail`, so `e_mail` and `EMailAddress` match) and plurals (`emails`), with the tokenizer splitting letters from digits so `email1` matches; carve-outs are keyed by claim, route, SURFACE and field, carry a justification, cover a synthesized HEAD under their GET, and a stale carve-out fails
SEC-3.note: Re-measured 2026-07-27 (node Phase A); the flat `proven` is now five obligations. The undeclared-parameter obligation is genuinely closed here and is `owed` in the sibling, which is each edition measured on its own mechanism rather than against the other. Findings: E-9, E-10, E-79.

obligations.name: the predicate rejects a registry match on a parameter it can see
obligations.text: Permanent refusal tests for a path parameter named for the value itself, a compound one, a snake-cased one and a query parameter.

obligations.name: the enumeration reaches every declared path and query parameter
obligations.text: Path parameters are reconciled between the URL text and `schema.params` and a disagreement in EITHER direction fails, so a parameter in the URL but not the schema is caught and so is the reverse. Query parameters come from a mandatory closed `schema.querystring`. Covered by the same narrowing measurement as SEC-1 (E-79).

obligations.name: a parameter that binds without being declared is inside the surface
obligations.text: This is the obligation the sibling carries as `owed`, and this edition closes it rather than inheriting it. `additionalProperties: false` plus Fastify's `removeAdditional` means an undeclared query parameter is STRIPPED before the handler runs, so an ad-hoc read of an undeclared parameter reads nothing. It does not close SEC-3's underlying harm, since a URL carrying PII still reaches logs and proxies whether or not the handler reads it; it closes the enumeration hole, which is what this obligation is.

obligations.name: the comparison resolves compounds, concatenations, decompositions and plurals of a listed word
obligations.text: Tokenized contiguous run, plus explicit entries for the three morphological classes a run over tokens cannot reach: concatenations (`firstname`, `dateofbirth`), decompositions (`mail`, so `e_mail` and `EMailAddress` match) and plurals (`emails`), with letters split from digits so `email1` matches. Its own false positives are ASSERTED rather than described: `fileName` and `tenantName` match and are accepted as the cost, `filename`, `namespace`, `mailbox` and `voicemail` do not.

obligations.name: carve-outs are reviewed and cannot rot
obligations.text: Keyed by claim, route, SURFACE and field, each carrying a justification, covering a synthesized HEAD under its GET, and a stale carve-out fails. The shipped list is empty, so both the suppression path and the staleness path were dead code an audit found shipped unexecuted; they are reachable now through the `carveOuts` parameter and both branches are exercised.

SEC-4.title: JWT hardening and revocation
SEC-4.mechanism: `server/src/platform/tokenVerification.ts` verifies a bearer token as a pure function over a token, a key set and an instant; `bearerCredential.ts` turns an Authorization header into a credential and applies the session-version check; `sessionVersions.ts` holds the server-side version; `composeApp` wires all three, and `tokenVerification.test.ts` proves them by input
SEC-4.note: Built 2026-07-27 at 53b1eec, and proved by INPUT rather than by configuration, because this stack has no validation object to read back off a host. That difference is not a handicap here: E-88 planted five of the sibling's seven validation properties permissive and all 261 of its tests stayed green, for want of a violating token to send. Every rejection below is asserted by REASON and not by status, for the reason E-90 gives: a refusal cannot distinguish a mechanism that works from one that is absent, because absence refuses everything, so only a success separates them. Findings: E-54, E-55, E-88, E-89, E-90.

obligations.name: the signing algorithm is pinned to exactly one
obligations.text: `ADMITTED_ALGORITHMS` is an exported frozen value asserted whole, not probed one exclusion at a time. E-54 is why: the sibling's pin was proven by minting one HS384 token, which says nothing about what the set ADMITS, and adding RS256 to it left its whole suite green. Planted 2026-07-27 at 53b1eec: HS384, HS512, RS256, ES256 and none are each refused with a reason naming the declared alg, and a token signed correctly with HS256 while DECLARING HS384 is refused for declaring it rather than for failing to verify, which is what makes this a comparison and not a negotiation.

obligations.name: tokens must be signed, on a branch the algorithm pin cannot shadow
obligations.text: Checked before the header is read at all, with its own reason. E-55 measured why the two must be independent: with the sibling's pin still `[HS256]` and `RequireSignedTokens` false, an alg:none token AUTHENTICATED, because an unsigned token never reaches signature validation so the pin never runs. Planted at 53b1eec: a token that is BOTH unsigned AND declares an inadmissible algorithm is refused for carrying no signature, which is the ordering the independence rests on.

obligations.name: the premise the claim rests on: tokens expire, and come from the configured issuer and audience
obligations.text: Recorded as its own obligation rather than folded into the ones above, because SEC-4's sentences name none of the three and this row should not pretend they do. E-88 is the argument: the revocation half says revocation takes effect `rather than at token expiry`, which PRESUPPOSES that tokens expire, and a guard set built from a claim's words alone does not cover a premise the claim states as background. Planted at 53b1eec: a wrong issuer, a wrong audience, an absent exp, a non-integer exp, a past exp and a future nbf are each refused by reason, and the exp boundary is asserted at one second so it is not off by one. Issuer and audience are read from resolved settings and never written twice (CFG-1, E-75).

obligations.name: a token minted before the current session version is refused
obligations.text: `decideCredential` compares the token's `sv` against the server-side version on every request that presents a token, and it is the only path by which `request.credential` is ever set, so there is no request that reaches a handler without passing it. Equality and not `>=`: a token minted AHEAD of the server's version is refused too, because it is one the server cannot account for. Planted at 53b1eec by disabling the comparison, which turned three tests red including the end-to-end one; and proven positively rather than only negatively, which E-90 says is the half that distinguishes a working gate from an absent one: the same token, the same server, 200 before the bump and 401 after it.

obligations.name: every principal carries a server-side version, and it is the server that carries it
obligations.text: The version lives in `sessionVersions.ts` on the server; the token carries only the version it was minted at, so no token can argue with a revocation. An unknown principal reads as `INITIAL_SESSION_VERSION`, which is asserted as a property rather than left to be discovered: a store with no user table behind it cannot distinguish a principal at version 1 from one it has never heard of, so any validly signed token bearing sv=1 for an unbumped subject is accepted. That is not a hole in revocation, which only has to invalidate what it has seen, and revoking requires having seen it; it is the absence of a principal store, which is a different claim and arrives with G.

obligations.name: revocation reaches every process serving the principal
obligations.text: The store is a Map inside one process. For the shape this edition ships, one process, revocation is immediate and is proven above. For any deployment that runs more than one, a bump reaches the process that received it and no other, so a revoked token keeps working everywhere else and the claim's word `immediately` is false of the system even though it is true of each process. Split out rather than argued away inside the obligation above, because someone seeding from this record will choose a replica count without reading a paragraph. trigger: the first deployment running more than one process, or the persistence layer, whichever lands first; the upgrade is a shared store behind the same `SessionVersions` interface. SEC-4's weakening note about a short-TTL cache attaches HERE and not before: there is no cache in front of a Map, so the revocation delay is currently zero and the note's named-and-tested-bound obligation has no surface yet.

SEC-5.title: No secrets in config
SEC-5.mechanism: the committed-config half IS built and proven: a secret-shaped key (token-matched against `SECRET_SHAPED`) may hold only the empty placeholder in a committed file, refused at resolution AND by `scanConfigurationSurface`; the dev store is at a path asserted to be outside `EDITION_ROOT`, which is a property of the path rather than of a gitignore; a lint confines filesystem reads to the settings seam; secret-shaped literals in source are reported, with an exemption list carrying a reason per entry and a staleness check
SEC-5.note: `owed` on the S-8 reasoning, deliberately and conservatively: two of the claim's obligations have no mechanism here. The vault port for runtime credentials is owed in both editions (trigger: first runtime credential). A credential assigned to a non-secret-shaped name is still invisible to both built halves, which is the name predicate's stated reach and E-9's shape in a fourth registry. The sibling's realization of the same claim is measurably weaker on the built half: see E-11 and E-12.

obligations.name: no secret-shaped value in committed configuration
obligations.text: a secret-shaped key (token-matched against `SECRET_SHAPED`) may hold only the empty placeholder in a committed file, refused both at resolution and by `scanConfigurationSurface`.

obligations.name: development secrets live outside the repository tree
obligations.text: the dev store sits at a path asserted to be outside `EDITION_ROOT`, which is a property of the path rather than of a gitignore, and a lint confines filesystem reads to the settings seam.

obligations.name: a CI secret-scan gate runs over the repository
obligations.text: `tools/secret-scan.mjs` runs in the CI loop with `--self-test` executed first, so the scan's extent is asserted in the same artifact as the scan (E-16). This obligation read `owed` in prose until 2026-07-26 and the E-16 repair had already built it (E-19).

obligations.name: runtime credentials sit behind a vault port
obligations.text: no runtime credential exists in this edition, so the port has nothing to hold and the stored-handle idiom has nothing to store (trigger: the first runtime credential).

SEC-6.title: Log safety
SEC-6.mechanism: `redact.ts` scrubs Authorization values (JSON and header forms) and JWT-shaped strings from harness output, unit-tested in `__tests__/redact.test.ts`
SEC-6.note: Measured in this edition's own tree 2026-07-27 (node Phase A, F2), not inferred from the sibling. Red-correct: narrowing the JWT arm to a pattern that matches nothing turns `scrubs a JWT-shaped token` red. The row is `owed` on its server half, and that half is trigger-gated rather than merely unbuilt: `createApp` constructs Fastify with `logger: false`, so this server emits no log at all. There is no logging surface to assert redaction over yet, which is a materially different situation from the sibling's and is why the trigger names the first log statement rather than a missing test.

obligations.name: secret-shaped values are scrubbed by one redactor
obligations.text: One redactor, three arms (JSON authorization, header authorization, JWT shape), red-correct when an arm is narrowed. Heuristic by shape, so a secret in a form none of the three arms matches escapes; each new secret shape owes its own arm.

obligations.name: each logging surface asserts its own redaction
obligations.text: The harness output surface is covered. The SERVER emits nothing: `createApp` passes `logger: false`. Trigger: the first server log statement, which creates the surface this obligation is about.

TIME-1.title: UTC, offset-aware, and nothing else
TIME-1.mechanism: the contract half IS built and proven: `scanEndpointSpine` walks every route's body, params, querystring, headers and response schemas and rejects a time-named property (token-matched against `TIME_SHAPED`) declared as a bare string, since `format: 'date-time'` is RFC3339 and RFC3339 requires an offset; `platform/clock.ts` is the one clock seam, with `new Date`, `Date.now`, `Date.parse`, `Date.UTC` and `performance.now` banned everywhere else by lint, which is the monotonic-durations extension's confinement
TIME-1.note: trigger: the first store, for the persistence surface, and the first scheduling slice, for the zone-carrying shape the weakening note describes. `owed` on the S-8 reasoning, and the claim itself does not port as written (A-5, B-5). A JS `Date` is an instant: it lacks the ambiguity the harm paragraph is about AND lacks the offset the statement requires, so it satisfies neither side of the ban, because "UTC-anchored offset-aware" fuses two properties `DateTimeOffset` supplies together. `Temporal` is absent from Node 24.13.1, asserted as a test. No persistence surface exists, so that third of the claim has nothing to scan; the response half of the contract scan is a report rather than a proof, because response schemas carry no closure obligation. The two editions check disjoint surfaces for this claim (E-15).

obligations.name: no naive instant on the contract surface
obligations.text: `scanEndpointSpine` walks every route's body, params, querystring, headers and response schemas and rejects a time-named property declared as a bare string, since `format: 'date-time'` is RFC3339 and RFC3339 requires an offset.

obligations.name: durations come from the monotonic source through one clock seam

The row's own note already admitted the duplication check's length floor while the status said `proven`, and the re-measurement found two live instances under it: the shared harness and smoke tools both default to a hardcoded port that duplicates `config/settings.json` (E-78). Not repaired here, because both files are COMPOSED SHARED files and the fix is the same cross-edition decision the sibling's `mintToken.mjs` needs (E-75); `edition.json` is now the obvious home for it, since DB2 established that pattern and it sits at the same relative path in both editions. The source checks run over the parsed AST rather than over text, because a text scan reported the comments explaining its own bans (E-5's second instance).

Values shorter than eight characters are excluded by a stated argument (a check that fires on `info` is a check somebody deletes), and non-string JSON values are never candidates at all, which is not a stated argument but a consequence of the type test. `http.port` is 5080, a number, so it is excluded twice over, and both the harness and the smoke tool carry `?? 'http://localhost:5080'` (E-78). That is a duplicated committed value AND the silent default CFG-1's own text calls out one claim over. CON-1.title: One wire dialect
CON-1.mechanism: none built. Route response shapes are declared per route in `src/routes/`, and nothing compares them against each other or against a dialect.
CON-1.note: Measured in this edition's own tree 2026-07-27 (node Phase A, F4), and the row was NOT correctly waiting. Its trigger read `the first enum on the wire`, which names the third of the claim's four clauses; the other three do not wait for an enum, and TWO OF THEM ARE VIOLATED IN SHIPPED CODE (E-83). `src/routes/notes.ts` declares and sends a bespoke `{ error: 'not found' }` 404 rather than problem details, with no host-level error handler for a route to conform to, and mints identifiers as `String(notes.size + 1)`, a dense sequential counter. A live violation is worse than an unbuilt guard, and this record showed neither. Repair is Phase B work: an error handler and an opaque id at the store boundary, and the store is what Phase B builds. Findings: E-83.

obligations.name: one host-level serialization and error configuration point
obligations.text: unbuilt AND unmet. `app.ts` registers no `setErrorHandler` and no shared error serializer, so each route decides its own error shape and there is nothing central for a scan to assert against. Trigger: a host-level error handler, which is the artifact this obligation is about.

obligations.name: no endpoint invents its own error shape
obligations.text: unbuilt, and VIOLATED in shipped code: the notes route declares `404: { type: 'object', properties: { error: { type: 'string' } } }` and sends `{ error: 'not found' }`, which is not RFC 9457 problem details (E-83). Trigger: the error handler above, then a scan over the composed route table's declared response shapes, which is cheap here because Fastify keeps the schema as a value on the route.

obligations.name: enums cross the wire as closed string sets
obligations.text: unbuilt, and this is the one clause whose subject genuinely does not exist yet: no route declares an enum. Trigger: the first enum on the wire. This trigger was the WHOLE row's trigger until this round, which is how the two violated clauses above stayed invisible.

obligations.name: identifiers are opaque strings
obligations.text: unbuilt, and VIOLATED in shipped code: `id: String(notes.size + 1)` is a dense sequential counter that satisfies the wire-type half of `opaque strings` and fails the opacity half (E-83). Adjacent to but not covered by SEC-7, which binds on anonymous surfaces and this route is gated. Trigger: an opaque id at the store boundary, then a scan over declared response shapes.

CON-2.title: Contract parity fixture
CON-2.mechanism: `client-web/src/data/__fixtures__/note-contract.fixture.json` is the one physical fixture; `noteContract.test.ts` asserts the client's `CreateNote`, `Note` and `NoteList` types against it, and `server/src/architecture/contractParity.ts` plus its test assert the server's declared route schemas and its emitted responses against the same file
CON-2.note: Producer half built 2026-07-27. E-82 recorded that nothing in `server/src` read the fixture, so the client was asserting against a second copy of its own beliefs; asking the server was the whole of the work and the answer was a live violation. `GET /notes` declared NO response schema at all and returned `{notes: [...]}` while the fixture and the client both say `{items, nextCursor}`, so the drift was not merely undetected, it was unreadable: a route that declares no response shape has nothing for a fixture to pin. Repaired in the same pass, with `cursor` added to the query schema because `removeAdditional` had been silently stripping the one the client sends, so every paged read answered page one. Findings: E-82, E-85, E-86.

obligations.name: exactly one corpus, physically one file
obligations.text: One fixture file inside the edition, read by the client test natively and by the server test through a relative path derived from `import.meta.dirname`. No copy exists inside the edition, so the claim's primary mechanism class holds here and the sanctioned materializer alternative is not needed: the precondition (both consumers under one root that travels together) is satisfied, because a seeded project's root holds both. Planted 2026-07-27 at 5dedb47 by removing the fixture: the server test file fails to load with ENOENT, so the read cannot go vacuous. Between EDITIONS the file is shared-tier and `compose.mjs --check` is the drift check, which is the alternative and is a different question from this one.

obligations.name: the consumer side asserts its types against the committed fixture
obligations.text: `noteContract.test.ts` reads the fixture off disk and checks every property name of the three client contract types against it, so a rename on the client fails the client build.

obligations.name: the producer side asserts its declared contracts against the same fixture
obligations.text: `contractParityFindings` is a pure function over the fixture and the composed route table, so eleven refusal tests assert that a defect is REPORTED rather than that the shipped tree is clean (the E-79 shape). Planted 2026-07-27 at 5dedb47: renaming `items` to `notes` in the list response turns exactly one test red naming both field sets, and nothing else in the suite notices. Every contract in the fixture must be bound by some route, so a corpus entry the server never answers for is red; that is half of what the sibling's equivalent obligation records as owed under E-60, and it flows back. Per-seam and not proven, measured the same day: because `noteResponse` is bound by two routes, DELETING the binding from `GET /notes/:noteId` leaves all 172 tests green, so a route can stop being pinned without anything reporting it. Trigger for the last of it: a rule deciding which response schemas MUST carry a binding, which needs a way to say that `/health` and the 404 shape are not hand-mirrored contracts.

obligations.name: what the server emits matches what it declares
obligations.text: Five request-level tests drive the composed app through `CreateAppSeams.authenticate` and assert the emitted field sets against the same fixture, plus the cursor walk's totality and the 403 for an insufficient credential. Built because the scan above pins the declaration only, and here a declaration and an emission are two objects: planted 2026-07-27 at 5dedb47, changing the handler's `return { items, nextCursor }` to `return { notes: items, nextCursor }` left the parity scan, tsc and eslint all clean while the server sent `{"nextCursor":null}` with the list gone from the wire (E-85). Per-seam: each new route carrying a mirrored contract owes its own emission test. The sibling has no equivalent obligation and does not need one, because its handler returns the typed record the contract IS.

obligations.name: every hand-mirrored contract is pinned by the corpus
obligations.text: The fixture-to-route direction binds (a corpus entry nothing answers for is reported), and the route-to-fixture direction does not: a fourth hand-mirrored contract added to both sides and never written into the fixture is invisible to every test in both trees, because a register cannot report what was never written into it. Trigger: a rule that decides membership of `hand-mirrored contract` from the code rather than from the register, which is the same trigger the sibling's row carries and is unbuilt in both editions.

DEP-1.title: Dependency quarantine

The row's own note already said the right thing, that the mechanism is realized in the shared tier and composed here so what is owed is the MEASUREMENT and not the build. The measurement is taken: four plants, all red-correct in this tree. Two obligations differ from the sibling's for a reason that is this edition's own and not a weakness: there is no container image anywhere in the tree, and `VERSIONS.md` says so in prose, so the image obligations are `latent` rather than `patterned`. The row stays `owed` on the single obligation neither edition has built, which needs a registry lookup no tool here makes. The window-number obligation is `proven` on the strongest evidence available: it caught a LIVE defect in this edition's own ledger on its first run (E-76).

Residues, unchanged: source mapping is deletable unreported, and publish dates are shape-tested rather than parsed.

This edition carries a real advisory-rule pin, so the obligation has a live subject rather than a control.

Proven on the strongest evidence a guard can have: on its first run it caught a live defect in THIS edition's ledger, which named the superseded window as a live one under a header declaring the current number (E-76, repaired).

TEST-2.title: E2E harness
TEST-2.mechanism: `client-web/tools/harness/main.ts` drives the real `src/data/notesRepo.ts` and `src/api/client.ts` against a running server and emits NDJSON; `tools/smoke/composedApp.smoke.ts` boots the composed entrypoint against the same server; `redact.ts` scrubs the output
TEST-2.note: Measured in this edition's own tree 2026-07-27 (node Phase A, F3), obligations 1 and 2 corrected the same day after the harness was RUN rather than read (E-84, E-87). The row said `trigger: the first client data service` and that trigger HAS FIRED: `client-web/src/data/notesRepo.ts` exists and the harness already drives it. What is missing is not the harness, it is a RUNNER. This edition has no e2e orchestrator (the sibling has `scripts/e2e.sh`) and its `ci.yml` has four jobs, none of which invokes the harness or the smoke. So the mechanism is shipped, wired as npm scripts, and started by nothing. Findings: E-80, E-84, E-87.

obligations.name: an out-of-process harness drives the real, unmodified client service layer
obligations.text: The harness exists and imports the real repository and client modules rather than reimplementing them. `latent` here means built and started by nothing: no orchestrator boots a server for it and no CI job runs it, so nothing re-runs it and any regression merges. It HAS now been executed once by hand, 2026-07-27 at 5dedb47, which is a measurement and not something the loop does: 1 of 7 scenarios green, the other six failing 401 because the credential mint is owed (SEC-4, TEN-6) and every gated route answers 401 by construction. The previous text said it had never been executed against a running server in this tree, and that is what running it corrected (E-84).

obligations.name: the floor is complete: every public method of every client data service has a scenario
obligations.text: The previous text read `unbuilt. The scenario list is hand-written`, and that was false about a file this edition ships: `main.ts` enumerates `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(NotesRepo.prototype)`, wraps every method to record what actually ran, and emits `service-method-coverage` as its own failing scenario line. It was watched doing exactly that on 2026-07-27, reporting `uncovered service methods: list, get, remove`. The status was right and the reason was wrong, which is E-87. Still `owed`, for the reason the sibling's row already carried and this one did not: the audit reads ONE class's prototype, so a second data service is invisible and a method declared as a class-field arrow function never enters the diffed set (E-67). Trigger: enumerate the class exports under `src/data/` rather than naming one, and enumerate instance members as well as prototype members.

obligations.name: the deterministic tier runs in CI
obligations.text: unbuilt. `ci.yml` runs the server suite, the client suite, docs-lint and secret-scan. It contains no harness or smoke step at all, so the e2e tier is not in the loop (E-80). Restated so it names a run that could pass rather than an artifact that could exist (E-84). trigger: a harness run that can be GREEN, which needs the credential mint (SEC-4, TEN-6) so the gated routes stop answering 401, and `DELETE /notes/:id`, which the client's `NotesRepo.remove` and the harness's `delete-note` scenario both already call and this server does not serve. Adding the job before those exists is a gate that is red on every run, and a red gate gets disabled rather than fixed.
